notes: Base plate was thickened to 2.41 mm to carry the two buried common layers.
The shoulder is the spring. A plug most of the dome wide left no shoulder to buckle; it is now small and thin, so most of the dome is free to snap.
The common strips show flush between the keys of a row. Nothing else lands on them, and a fingertip on one only touches the output.

Every key shorts its top half pad to its bottom half pad. The top halves are the nodes of a printed resistor chain, the bottom halves all sit on a buried common plane that IS the output, so one pin reads the whole grid.

circuit.title: LADDER KEYPAD
lines: Three wires. VCC pad to 3V3, GND pad to ground, OUT pad to one ADC pin. Then one resistor: 100 k from the OUT pin to ground.

You do not build a voltage divider: the keypad IS the divider. The printed chain of 12 equal resistors runs from VCC down to GND, and every key connects a different point of that chain to OUT. Key 1 sits at the top and reads nearly 3V3, the last key sits one step above ground.

The 100 k pull down does one job: with no key pressed OUT is connected to nothing, and the resistor holds it at 0 V so no key reads zero. It has to be much larger than the chain's 211.08 kohm or it drags the upper keys down; that is why it is 100 k and not 10 k.
Decode: read the ADC, compare against 13 thresholds set halfway between the 13 expected levels (0, then 12 steps of about 85 counts). Take a few samples and require two the same to debounce.
circuit.formula: V(key k) = 3.3 x (12 - k + 1) / 12, no key = 0 V

notes: The shoulder is the spring. The old design put a plug most of the dome wide on the ceiling, which left a rim of shoulder too narrow to buckle; the plug is now small and under a millimetre thick, so most of the dome is free to snap.

Two printed contacts meeting face to face is a rough junction with a thin oxide and polymer skin, so closed resistance lands anywhere from a couple of kilohms to tens of kilohms and it drifts with wipe count. Read it as a logic input with a pullup, never as a current path.
The plug is deliberately not wired to anything. It rides on the dome and bridges the two half pads only while you are pressing.

The plug is in the conductive TPU slot on purpose: printed on the underside of a TPU ceiling it fuses to the dome, where a PLA puck would peel off. Its contact resistance is higher than PLA, which is fine for a switch read against a pullup.

circuit.title: THINPOT
lines: T1 to ground, T3 to 3V3, T2 (the collector) to the ADC, exactly like a pot. Add 100 k from T2 to ground: with nothing pressing, the collector floats, and the pull down parks it at zero so untouched reads as untouched.

Pressed, the collector taps the track and the ADC reads the position as a fraction of 3V3. The track is 4.17 kohm, so the 100 k pull down bends the top of the range by a couple of percent; use 1 M or a buffer if that matters.
Contact resistance is a few kohm and drops out of the position reading because almost nothing flows through the collector.
circuit.formula: V = 3.3 x position along the track, 0 V untouched
